```{r}
#| label: initial-setup
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

# Data importation (raw tables, cleaned later)
eige_raw     <- read_csv("data/wmid_natparl.csv") # Proportion of women in national parliaments
renew_raw    <- read_csv("data/nrg_ind_ren.csv") # Share of renewable energies
spend_raw    <- read_csv("data/gov_10a_exp.csv") # Public spending on environmental protection
tax_raw      <- read_csv("data/env_ac_tax.csv") # Environmental taxes
paygap_raw   <- read_csv("data/sdg_05_20.csv") # Pay gap between women and men
election_raw <- read_csv("data/view_election.csv") # Elections
party_raw    <- read_csv("data/view_party.csv") # Political parties

# Reference table of the 27 EU Member States 
eu27 <- tribble( # Manually created table with 2 columns : country name and its associated Eurostat code
  ~country,      ~code, # "~" allows to declare the column names
  "Austria",     "AT", "Belgium",    "BE", "Bulgaria",   "BG",
  "Croatia",     "HR", "Cyprus",     "CY", "Czechia",    "CZ",
  "Denmark",     "DK", "Estonia",    "EE", "Finland",    "FI",
  "France",      "FR", "Germany",    "DE", "Greece",     "EL",
  "Hungary",     "HU", "Ireland",    "IE", "Italy",      "IT",
  "Latvia",      "LV", "Lithuania",  "LT", "Luxembourg", "LU",
  "Malta",       "MT", "Netherlands","NL", "Poland",     "PL",
  "Portugal",    "PT", "Romania",    "RO", "Slovakia",   "SK",
  "Slovenia",    "SI", "Spain",      "ES", "Sweden",     "SE"
)

years <- 2007:2022 # Creation of a vector with the years that interest us
```


# Project repository

All the code and the raw data of this project are available on GitHub:
<https://github.com/leelougrandmougin-rgb/project-dm-environment-parliament-eu>

# Research question

Women’s presence in European national parliaments has increased steadily since the mid-2000s (EIGE, 2019), part of a broader rise of women in governance worldwide that has led academics to ask whether women make different political decisions than men (Salamon, 2022). This raises a question about representation: does having more women among elected members change what parliaments decide? We study one policy area, the environment, and ask: do EU member states with a higher share of women in parliament have stronger environmental policies, and does the same pattern appear within countries over time, between 2007 and 2022?

Environmental policy is an interesting case for two reasons. First, it can be measured in several comparable ways across EU countries. Second, it is not a traditional “women’s issue”, so it tests whether women’s presence matters beyond such issues (Salamon, 2022).

We look at the 27 current EU member states, observed yearly (432 country-years). With so few countries, we adopt a longitudinal design. The period starts in 2007 because it is when EU leaders set the 2020 climate and energy targets, and EIGE data are incomplete before that year.

We measure environmental policy at three levels: an outcome (the share of renewables in gross final energy consumption), an input (public spending on environmental protection, as a share of GDP) and an instrument (environmental tax revenues, as a share of GDP). Each is a dependent variable and none is treated as the main one. We read higher values as stronger policy, although this is a simplification (tax revenues, for instance, also depend on energy consumption).

Our main hypothesis is that countries with a higher share of women in parliament also score higher on these three indicators. We expect this association to be weaker in countries with more gender inequality, where elected women may have to adopt dominant masculine norms to succeed. We measure gender inequality with the gender pay gap, used as a control and also to split countries into more and less gender-equal groups, based on each country’s average for the 2007-2010 period. We also expect to observe the same pattern within countries: in years when the share of women in a given country is above its own average, the corresponding indicators should also be higher.

An alternative explanation could be that the link comes from parties rather than from the gender of members: green parties may elect more women and also push for environmental policies. We therefore control for the green seat share in the lower house.

Our strategy relies on linear regressions on the country-year panel. We first compare countries with each other, regressing each indicator on the share of women, with year dummies to remove shocks common to all countries, and adding the green seat share and the pay gap as controls step by step. We then add an interaction with the “more gender-equal” group. To check whether the pattern also holds over time, we split each country’s share of women into its period average and its yearly deviation, which gives between-country and within-country estimates in one model. Plots and descriptive statistics complete the analysis.

Finally, an association is not a causal effect: countries with more women differ in many other ways, such as wealth (which we do not control for), political culture or natural resources, and the indicators also depend on energy prices, crises and EU-level targets. With only 27 countries, each observed 16 times, standard errors are likely too small, so significance should be read as indicative only.



# Data sources

## How to obtain the data

The table below gives for each source: the link to the data, the filters used, and the download date.

For Eurostat, we opened the table in the Eurostat Data Browser, applied the filters listed below, and exported the result as a CSV file. EIGE (a CSV file) and ParlGov
(a ZIP archive of CSV tables) were downloaded in full. The selection of the variables and period used in the analysis is described in the data cleaning section.

| Source | Data | Filters at download | Download date |
|---|---|---|---|
| EIGE | [wmid_natparl](https://eige.europa.eu/gender-statistics/dgs/indicator/wmidm_pol_parl__wmid_natparl) | None (full table downloaded). | 2026-10-22 |
| Eurostat | [nrg_ind_ren](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nrg_ind_ren/default/table?lang=en) | `nrg_bal` = REN, `unit` = PC, `geo` = the 27 EU Member States, from 2004. | 2026-10-22 |
| Eurostat | [gov_10a_exp](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/gov_10a_exp/default/table) | `sector` = S13, `cofog99` = GF05, `na_item` = TE, `unit` = PC_GDP, `geo` = the 27 EU Member States, from 2004. | 2026-10-22 |
| Eurostat | [env_ac_tax](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_tax/default/table) | `unit` = PC_GDP, `geo` = the 27 EU Member States, from 2004 (all tax types). | 2026-10-22 |
| Eurostat | [sdg_05_20](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sdg_05_20/default/table?lang=en) | `nace_r2` = B-S_X_O, `unit` = PC, `geo` = the 27 EU Member States, all years (2007–2022). | 2026-11-17 |
| ParlGov | [parlgov.org](https://parlgov.org/data-info/) | None (full archive downloaded, November 2023 version). | 2026-10-23 |


## Description of the sources

**EIGE.** The European Institute for Gender Equality (EIGE) is an EU agency. Its Gender Statistics Database collects data on the number of women and men in decision-making positions. The table "National parliaments: presidents and members" (*wmid_natparl*) counts women and men among the members and the presidents of national parliaments, for the single or lower house, the upper house and both houses combined. It is a quarterly data set covering `r n_distinct(eige_raw$geo)` countries and aggregates, from `r substr(min(eige_raw$time), 1, 4)` to `r substr(max(eige_raw$time), 1, 4)`. Each row corresponds to a combination of country, quarter, chamber, position, sex and unit (absolute number or percentage). The share of women in the single or lower house is our explanatory variable.

**Eurostat.** Eurostat is the statistical office of the European Union, and its data are harmonized across Member States. We used four annual data sets: 

- *nrg_ind_ren* : share of renewable energy in gross final energy consumption, the indicator used to express the EU targets for 2020 and 2030. It measures the outcome of environmental policies.
- *gov_10a_exp* : general government expenditure by function (COFOG classification), here on environmental protection, as a percentage of GDP. It measures the budgetary effort. 
- *env_ac_tax* : environmental tax revenues from national accounts, by category (energy, transport, pollution and resources), as a percentage of GDP. It measures a fiscal instrument voted by parliaments. 

- *sdg_05_20* : unadjusted gender pay gap, defined as the difference between the average gross hourly earnings of men and women, as a percentage of men's earnings. It covers firms with ten employees or more, in industry, construction and services (except public administration, defense and compulsory social security). It is based on the Structure of Earnings Survey, which takes place every four years, with national estimates for the years in between. 

**ParlGov.** ParlGov (Parliaments and Governments database) is an academic database compiled from official and secondary sources. It documents elections, parties and cabinets in European and OECD democracies. The version used here is the November 2023 archive, made of 33 CSV tables. We used two of them: 

- *view_election* : number of seats won by each party at each election. 
- *view_party* : political family of each party. 

Combined, they give the share of seats held by green parties, our second control variable.


## Data files

```{r}
#| label: file-tables
#| results: asis

# We build one table per data file
# d: The data frame
# file: Its path
# content: Short description
# time: The column with dates (NULL if none)
# area: The column with countries

file_info <- function(d, file, content, time = NULL, area) {
  tibble(
    Item  = c("File", "Content", "Rows", "Columns", "Period", "Countries / entities"),
    Value = c(file, content,
              format(nrow(d), big.mark = ","), # Number of rows
              ncol(d), # Number of columns
              if (is.null(time)) "Not applicable" else paste(range(substr(time, 1, 4)), collapse = " to "), # Period : first and last year (4 first digits of the date), or "Not applicable" if no dates available
              n_distinct(area)) # Number of different countries
  )
}

# We store each table in a list
tables <- list(
  "EIGE: women in national parliaments" =
    file_info(eige_raw, "data/wmid_natparl.csv",
              "Number or percentage of women and men in national parliaments, by quarter",
              eige_raw$time, eige_raw$geo),
  "Eurostat: renewable energy share" =
    file_info(renew_raw, "data/nrg_ind_ren.csv",
              "Share of renewable energy in gross final energy consumption (%)",
              renew_raw$TIME_PERIOD, renew_raw$geo),
  "Eurostat: government spending on environmental protection" =
    file_info(spend_raw, "data/gov_10a_exp.csv",
              "General government expenditure on environmental protection (% of GDP)",
              spend_raw$TIME_PERIOD, spend_raw$geo),
  "Eurostat: environmental taxes" =
    file_info(tax_raw, "data/env_ac_tax.csv",
              "Environmental tax revenues (% of GDP)",
              tax_raw$TIME_PERIOD, tax_raw$geo),
  "Eurostat: gender pay gap" =
    file_info(paygap_raw, "data/sdg_05_20.csv",
              "Unadjusted gender pay gap (% of men's hourly earnings)",
              paygap_raw$TIME_PERIOD, paygap_raw$geo),
  "ParlGov: election results" =
    file_info(election_raw, "data/view_election.csv",
              "Seats won by each party at each election",
              election_raw$election_date, election_raw$country_name),
  "ParlGov: parties" =
    file_info(party_raw, "data/view_party.csv",
              "Political family of each party",
              area = party_raw$country_name)
)

# Finally, we print the tables one after the other
for (i in seq_along(tables)) { # One loop per table
  title <- names(tables)[i] # Get the title of the table number "i"
  if (i > 1) cat("\n\n&nbsp;")   # Blank line between a table and the next title
  cat("\n\n**", sub(":.*", "", title), "**:", sub("^[^:]*:", "", title), "\n\n", sep = "") # Title in bold, the rest in normal font
  cat(kable(tables[[i]]), sep = "\n") # kable() turns the tibble into a markdown table, cat() writes it in the document
}
```


# Most important variables

We only describe here the variables used in our analysis, those used to select the relevant rows, and those used to join the different data sets.

**Explanatory variable**: share of women in national parliaments (from `wmid_natparl`).

- *Analysis*: `value` gives this share once the right rows have been selected. This column contains either a number of people or a percentage, depending on the `UNIT`.
- *Selection*: `UNIT`, `EGROUP`, `POSITION` and `sex` (the unit, chamber, position and sex of each `value`) allow us to identify the rows giving the percentage of women among the members of the single or lower house.
- *Join*: `geo` and `time`, country name and quarter of observation.

**Dependent variables**: renewable energy, environmental spending and taxes (from `nrg_ind_ren`, `gov_10a_exp` and `env_ac_tax`).

- *Analysis*: `OBS_VALUE` gives the share of renewable energy in gross final energy consumption (%) in `nrg_ind_ren`, the general government expenditure on environmental protection (% of GDP) in `gov_10a_exp`, and the environmental tax revenue (% of GDP) in `env_ac_tax`.
- *Selection*: `tax` (actual category of environmental tax) in `env_ac_tax` allows us to identify the rows giving the total environmental taxes.
- *Join*: `geo` and `TIME_PERIOD`, country name and year of observation.

**Control variables**: gender pay gap and share of green seats in national parliaments (from `sdg_05_20`, `view_election` and `view_party`).

- *Analysis*: `OBS_VALUE` gives the unadjusted gender pay gap (%) in `sdg_05_20`, while the share of seats held by green parties is computed from `seats` and `seats_total` (both from `view_election`) and `family_name_short` (from `view_party`, where `eco` identifies the green parties).
- *Selection*: `election_type` (the type of election, national or European Parliament) in `view_election` allows us to identify the rows of national parliamentary elections.
- *Join*: `geo` and `TIME_PERIOD` in `sdg_05_20` (country code and year), `country_name` and `election_date` in `view_election` (country and date of the election), and `party_id` in `view_election` and `view_party` (identifier of a party).


# Joining and cleaning

The sources differ in observation frequency (quarterly for EIGE, annual for Eurostat, election-based for ParlGov) and in the way countries are named.
Then, in the following sections we first clean each source separately before matching all of them by country and year.

## EIGE

We keep the percentage of women among the members of the single or lower house for the current 27 Member States and for the period 2007–2022. The quarterly values are averaged to get one value per year.

```{r}
#| label: clean-eige

# It keeps the share of women (in %) among the members of the single or lower house, for the EU27
women_q <- eige_raw |>
  filter(`_UNIT` == "PC", `_EGROUP` == "PARL_SINGLOW",
         `_POSITION` == "MEMB_PARL", `_sex` == "W",
         geo %in% eu27$country) |>
    mutate(year = as.integer(str_sub(time, 1, 4))) |>  # Years are defined as the first 4 characters of the quarter (converted to integers)
  filter(year %in% years)

women <- women_q |>
  group_by(country = geo, year) |> # Renaming "geo" to "country" in order to harmonize the column names across the tables
  summarise(women = mean(value), .groups = "drop") # We take the average of the quarters of each year to get one final value per country and year
```

The quarter 2007-Q3 is missing for all countries, so the mean of 2007 uses only three values.

## Eurostat

For the three indicators, we keep the 27 Member States and the period 2007-2022. 
For `env_ac_tax`, we only keep the total of environmental taxes.

```{r}
#| label: clean-eurostat

clean_eurostat <- function(d) { # Following function is used to clean every Eurostat table
  d |>
    filter(geo %in% eu27$country, TIME_PERIOD %in% years) |>
    select(country = geo, year = TIME_PERIOD, value = OBS_VALUE) # It keep and renames 3 columns, with the same names for the three tables
}

# Then we apply the previous function to our three indicators, and rename each value column after its indicator
renew  <- clean_eurostat(renew_raw) |> rename(renewables = value)
spend  <- clean_eurostat(spend_raw) |> rename(env_spending = value)
envtax <- tax_raw |>
    filter(tax == "Total environmental taxes") |>  # It only keeps the total (as it removes the rows of the other non useful categories)
  clean_eurostat() |>
  rename(env_tax = value)
```

## Gender pay gap

First, we convert the country codes to country names (with `eu27`). Then, we average the pay gap over 2007–2010 for each country and compare it to the median of the 27 countries: below the median means that the country is "more gender-equal", and above it means "less gender-equal".

```{r}
#| label: clean-paygap

# First thing first is that we convert each country codes to names (e.g. "EL" to "Greece") ; we also keep our study period 2007-2022
paygap <- paygap_raw |>
  left_join(eu27, by = c("geo" = "code")) |> # We link each country code to its name using the "eu27" table
  filter(TIME_PERIOD %in% years) |>
  select(country, year = TIME_PERIOD, pay_gap = OBS_VALUE) # We keep "country" (from eu27) and rename the year and value columns

# In this part we compute the mean pay gap of each country over 2007-2010 and compare it with the median of the 27 countries
equality_groups <- paygap |>
  filter(year <= 2010) |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarise(gap_2007_2010 = mean(pay_gap, na.rm = TRUE)) |> # We create a new variable that is the mean pay gap of each country over 2007-2010 (we didn't forget to ignore the missing values)
  mutate(equality_group = case_when( # We create another new variable that classifies each country relative to the median of the 27 countries
  gap_2007_2010 <  median(gap_2007_2010, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "more gender-equal",
  gap_2007_2010 >= median(gap_2007_2010, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "less gender-equal")) 
```

## ParlGov

We only keep the national parliamentary elections (and not the European ones).
We also recode "Czech Republic" to "Czechia" (which is the name used in the other sources).
We then join our two ParlGov tables (`view_election` and `view_party`) by `party_id` in order to:

- get the political family of each party (not present in `view_election`);
- compute for each election the share of seats of the single or lower house held by green parties (`eco`).

Finally, for each year, we take the last election held on or before 31 December (in order to keep our result until the next election).

```{r}
#| label: clean-parlgov

# Share of seats held by green parties at each national election of the EU27
green <- election_raw |>
  filter(election_type == "parliament") |>
  mutate(country = recode(country_name, "Czech Republic" = "Czechia")) |>  # It creates "country" from "country_name", renaming "Czech Republic" to "Czechia" as in the other sources
  filter(country %in% eu27$country) |>
  left_join(select(party_raw, party_id, family_name_short), by = "party_id") |>   # We join the party family from "view_party" to each election row of "view election", using "party_id"
  group_by(country, election_date) |>
  summarise(green_share = 100 * sum(seats[family_name_short %in% "eco"], na.rm = TRUE) /  # We sum here without using filter() (as elections without green party must stay in the table, with 0 % !)
                            max(seats_total, na.rm = TRUE), # "seats_total" is repeated on every party row of an election, so max() keeps one copy of it
            .groups = "drop")

green_year <- expand_grid(country = eu27$country, year = years) |>
  mutate(year_end = as.Date(paste0(year, "-12-31"))) |> # We build the date "31 December" of each year, so that the elections of that year are included in the comparison
  left_join(green, by = join_by(country, closest(year_end >= election_date))) |> # We join to each country-year the green share of its latest election (up to 31 December)
  select(country, year, green_share) # We keep the keys country and year and the green share
```

## Final panel

To obtain our final panel (one row per country and year), we join all the cleaned tables by country and year, starting from a table with every combination of our 27 countries and 16 years.

```{r}
#| label: panel
country_year <- expand_grid(country = eu27$country, year = years) # It creates all the possible combinations with our countries and years (27 x 16 = 432 rows) - which is slightly useful because eventual missing data in a source will give an NA when joining (instead of removing the row !)

# Then we join to it each previous cleaned table, matching on country and year
panel <- country_year |>
  left_join(women,  by = c("country", "year")) |>
  left_join(renew,  by = c("country", "year")) |>
  left_join(spend,  by = c("country", "year")) |>
  left_join(envtax, by = c("country", "year")) |>
  left_join(paygap, by = c("country", "year")) |>
  left_join(green_year, by = c("country", "year")) |>
  left_join(select(equality_groups, country, equality_group), by = "country")  # We also add the equality group for each country (this means that need to remove "gap_2007_2010", used only to build the group, and we perform the matching by country, since the group is defined only once per country)

stopifnot(nrow(panel) == 432)  # It stops with an error if the joins duplicated or if there are lost rows (we expect exactly 432 rows) 
```

## Missing values

We decided to keep the missing values as missing (rather than imputing them). They concern three variables:

- `env_spending` (Eurostat): Slovakia has no data for the period 2007–2009.
- `pay_gap` (Eurostat): Croatia has 6 missing years and Greece has 10.
- `seats` (ParlGov): missing for a few parties in Cyprus (2021), Hungary (2010–2022) and Poland (2007). They are ignored in the sum of seats (`na.rm = TRUE`), which does not affect the green share since none of them belongs to the green family.

The other variables (women in parliament, renewables, environmental taxes, green share and the equality group) are complete for the 432 country-years. The table below counts the missing values of the panel by country and variable.


# Target variables

Our target variables are our three dependent variables, which we treat equally: the share of renewable energy in gross final energy consumption (outcome), public spending on environmental protection (input) and environmental tax revenues (instrument).

```{r}
#| label: target-plot
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5
long_panel <- panel |>
  pivot_longer(c(renewables, env_spending, env_tax), # We reshape to one row per country, year and indicator, so that ggplot can draw one plot per indicator
               names_to = "indicator", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(indicator = factor(indicator, # We set the order of the plots and we give them titles
                            levels = c("renewables", "env_spending", "env_tax"),
                            labels = c("Renewables (% of energy consumption)",
                                       "Environmental spending (% of GDP)",
                                       "Environmental taxes (% of GDP)")))

# We also compute (and will represent it) the mean of the 27 countries as a benchmark
eu_mean <- long_panel |>
  group_by(indicator, year) |>
  summarise(value = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")  # We ignore the missing values

selected_countries <- c("Sweden", "Germany", "Poland", "Malta")  # We choose a few countries from different parts of the EU to follow their trajectories (in colour)

ggplot(long_panel, aes(x = year, y = value, group = country)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey40", aplha = 0.6) +  # We draw each of the 27 countries in grey (semi-transparent, to see where lines overlap)
  geom_line(data = eu_mean, aes(group = 1), colour = "black", linewidth = 1.4) +  # We draw the mean in black
  facet_wrap(~ indicator, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +  #  We draw one plot per indicator, each with its own vertical scale (since the units and levels differ)
  labs(title = "Environmental policy indicators in the EU, 2007–2022",
       subtitle = "27 countries (grey) and mean of the 27 countries (black)",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +  # We remove the axis titles and the legend title (in order to make the overall figure more readable)
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
